query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A reactive surface modification that forms an in situ, self-lubricating tribolayer will stabilize the coefficient of friction and reduce wear of the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy over the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk, single‐phase CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy (produced, for example, by additive manufacturing or conventional casting/thermomechanical treatment) with a relatively coarse microstructure that shows strong temperature‐dependent wear and friction behavior.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, reactive surface coating (or introduce a surface treatment) engineered to promote the formation of a nanostructured, lubricious tribolayer during sliding. This coating is designed to react with the environment and frictional heat so that an amorphous or finely nanocrystallized oxide/intermetallic phase develops in situ.
generation.conditions: Sliding (e.g., pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk) tests performed in ambient atmosphere under variable loads and sliding speeds, with test temperatures ramped from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an adaptive, nanocomposite tribofilm (composed of self-organized amorphous oxides and/or interfacial phases) that refines dynamically under shear.
generation.mechanism: Under friction, the reactive coating chemically interacts with ambient oxygen and the frictional heat to produce a stable, lubricious surface layer. This in situ tribolayer reduces shear strength and minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact (thus lowering adhesive wear) while compensating for temperature-induced variations in deformation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated/intervention samples will maintain a relatively low and stable friction coefficient and exhibit significantly reduced wear rates across the entire temperature span from RT to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The starting CoCrFeNi material, which shows variable friction and wear—often increasing friction coefficient and wear rates at certain temperatures due to inadequate surface protection and temperature-induced microstructural changes.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under dry or mildly oxidizing conditions in sliding contacts with typical industrial loads and speeds over the temperature range of 25 to 800 °C. Its performance may need re-evaluation if the environment (e.g., highly corrosive or ultra-high vacuum) substantially alters the oxidation kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal coating composition, thickness, and processing parameters still require determination. The long-term durability of the in situ tribolayer under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads is also uncertain and must be validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one group with the reactive surface coating and one uncoated control group. Using a pin-on-disk tribometer, run sliding tests under identical very controlled conditions (same load, sliding speed, and ambient atmosphere) at incremental temperatures spanning from room temperature to 800 °C. Record the steady-state friction coefficients and wear rates for each temperature step.
measurements: Wear volume (or specific wear rate) vs temperature
Post-test surface microstructure and tribolayer composition via SEM/EDS/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not display statistically significant lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range compared to the uncoated controls, or if the adaptive tribolayer fails to form or remain stable, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation. The microstructural characteristics of the AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings after the high temperature wear resistance test shows a highly favorable impact on microstructure stability and wear resistance, due to its the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetallic compounds.
